## ORIGINAL

A consensus of international experts on definition, sampling, treatment, and prevention of peripheral extracorporeal membrane oxygenation cannula‑site infection obtained by the Delphi method: the SAVECMO study

Paul Masi1, Darryl Abrams2, Ali Ait Hssain3, Martin Balik4, Nicholas A. Barrett5,6, Lars Mikael Broman7,8, Luigi Camporota5,6, Yih‑Sharng Chen9, Alain Combes10,11, Daniel De Backer12, Lorenzo Del Sorbo13, Rodrigo Diaz14, Dirk W. Donker15, Ghislaine Douflé16, Eddy Fan17, John F. Fraser18,19, Marco Giani20, Raphael Giraud21, Giacomo Grasselli22,23, Sami Hraiech24, Roberto Lorusso25, Graeme MacLaren26, Joseph E. Marcus27,28, Gennaro Martucci29, Pedro Vitale Mendes30, Shinichiro Ohshimo31, José‑Artur Paiva32,33,34, Sunghoon Park35, Kollengode Ramanathan36, Jordi Riera37,38, Roberto Roncon‑Albuquerque Jr.39, Leonardo Salazar40, Matthieu Schmidt10,11, Aditya Shah41, Kiran Shekar42, Alexander Supady43,44, Fabio Silvio Taccone45, Joseph E. Tonna46,47, Pauline Yeung Ng48, Hakeem Yusuff49 and Charles‑Edouard Luyt10,11*  For EuroELSO

Abstract Background:  Nosocomial infections are common in patients receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), with ECMO cannula-site infections (ECMO-CSI) being the most frequent infections directly related to the ECMO run. These infections can significantly impact patient outcomes. Currently, no adult guidelines exist for the prevention, diagnosis, and/or treatment of peripheral ECMO-CSI, resulting in heterogeneity in both clinical practice and research findings. Methods:  We conducted a Delphi study involving 39 international experts in ECMO management. The experts participated in four Delphi rounds to reach consensus on various aspects of ECMO-CSI complicating peripheral ECMO (central ECMO excluded), including definition, clinical suspicion, diagnostic methods, preventive measures, and treat‑ ment. Consensus was defined as ≥ 70% agreement among experts on each proposed item.

Results:  The Delphi process established consensus on key aspects of ECMO-CSI. Experts agreed on clinical scenarios that warrant suspicion of ECMO-CSI, such as purulent discharge and local inflammatory signs. Standardized sampling techniques, including swabs and purulent drainage aspiration, were recommended, while others were rejected. Definitions were clarified, specifying that ECMO-CSI is defined by the isolation of a pathogen through local microbio‑ logical sampling and the presence of purulent discharge or local inflammatory signs. Among the preventive meas‑ ures, the use of chlorhexidine-impregnated or semipermeable polyurethane dressings, unchanged for 7 days unless soiled or bleeding, was recommended, whereas systematic antibiotic prophylaxis, even for surgical ECMO, was not recommended. Conclusion:  This study presents an international expert consensus focusing on peripheral ECMO-CSI, providing a standardized framework to improve clinical management and facilitate future research. The consensus aims to enhance patient outcomes and support evidence-based guidelines in this complex field. Keywords:  Delphi, Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), Cannula-site infection (CSI), Treatment, Definition, Prevention

## Introduction

The increasing use of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for respiratory and/or cardiac support has been accompanied by a growing incidence of nosocomial infections, which significantly worsen patient outcomes and are associated with increased morbidity and mortality [1]. Among these infections, ECMO cannula-site infections (CSI) are frequent, with incidences ranging from 0 to 17.2 episodes/1000 ECMO days [2–4]. These infections can lead to prolonged hospital stays, increased healthcare costs, and are associated with higher mortality rate. Diagnosing ECMO-CSI can be challenging: because of the extracorporeal circuit, general clinical signs (e.g., fever) may be absent, while patients on ECMO often present with a nonspecific inflammatory syndrome. Similarly, treatment of ECMO-CSI can be also challenging: unlike central venous lines, which can be easily removed and replaced, ECMO cannulas are generally critical for maintaining adequate life support. Decannulation or change of cannula site can be extremely difficult and may not always be feasible, complicating the management of these infections. Currently, there is a lack of clear definitions and treatment guidelines for ECMO-CSI in adults [1–3, 5–20]. Existing recommendations do not adequately address which samples should be collected, the characteristics of these infections, or the treatment modalities. Furthermore, there is often confusion between bloodstream infections (BSI) and ECMO-CSI, leading to inconsistencies in diagnosis and treatment approaches. We aimed to achieve a consensus definition of peripheral ECMO-CSI, including prevention, methodology of microbiological sampling, and treatment. Subsequently, our goals are to improve the management of ECMO-CSI by physicians and facilitate the harmonization of clinical practice and study outcomes for future trials.

Methods Selection of the expert panel In October 2024, we sent an invitation to participate in the survey, to 48 international experts working in Intensive Care Units (ICU) selected by the scientific committee (P.M. and C-E. L.). Experts were selected on the basis of their clinical experience (a minimum of 5 years of experience as a senior physician treating ECMO patients and working in a medium- or high-volume ECMO center [21]); on their interest in the field, reflected by their publications (at least 5 publications in ECMO field as first or last authors); and/or expertise in formulating ECMO guidelines. To avoid overrepresentation and ensure international balance, expert selection was limited to four per country. The expert panel consisted of 39 international experts (response rate: 81%). The map of represented countries is shown in Supplemental Fig.  S1, and the experts are listed in Supplemental Table S1. Completion of the online surveys was considered as implied consent to participate in the Delphi process. None of the experts was aware of the list of participants in the expert panel and could not consult each other before replying.

Delphi process The Delphi rounds were prepared by the scientific committee of the study (P.M. and C-E. L.). Each round of

Take home message

This Delphi study establishes an international expert consensus on cannula-site infections during peripheral ECMO, addressing critical gaps in definition, diagnosis, and prevention. By standardizing clini‑ cal suspicion criteria, sampling techniques, and preventive meas‑ ures—such as chlorhexidine dressings—while discouraging routine antibiotic prophylaxis, it provides a pragmatic framework to reduce practice heterogeneity. These evidence-based recommendations aim to improve patient outcomes and guide future research, filling a void in current ECMO management guidelines.

questions was delivered anonymously by e-mail to ensure that none of the experts knew the identity of any of the other experts or their responses. E-mail reminders were sent until all members of the expert panel had answered each round of questions. The process was supervised by one of the investigators (P.M.). The questions included were in multiple-choice format or were based on a sevenpoint Likert scale to quantify the degree of agreement between respondents. A space for comment was left after each question, and the comments made were used to refine the questionnaires for the following round. The results were analyzed by the scientific committee after each round and summary reports describing aggregate group responses were sent to experts to enable them to modify their responses to the questions in the next round. Successive iterations of the Delphi questionnaire were administered to all experts until a consensus was obtained [22, 23]. Consensus was defined as agreement (score 5–7) or disagreement (scores 1–3) with the Likertscale statements, or a particular choice made by more than 70% of the experts for the multiple-choice questions as in the latest intensive care studies [24–27]. Questions for which no consensus was obtained after two rounds were removed and other fields of interest were discussed. The process followed is shown in Supplemental Fig. S2. Importantly, the experts were informed that the questions concerned both VA and VV ECMO, regardless of cannulation site (jugular or femoral), and regardless of whether cannulation was surgical or percutaneous, unless otherwise specified. Moreover, the experts were aware that the questions related only to peripheral ECMO, and not to central ECMO.

Literature review The questions were developed based on a preliminary literature review. We searched for publications (on Pub- Med, English language, from 01/01/2005 to 04/06/2025) on ECMO-CSI, using the following keywords: ((CRI [MeSH Terms]) OR (cannula related infection [MeSH Terms]) OR (CSI [MeSH Terms]) OR (cannula site infection [MeSH Terms]) OR (cannula infection [MeSH Terms]) OR (infection [MeSH Terms]) OR (complication [MeSH Terms])) AND ((ECMO) OR (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation) OR (ECLS) OR (extracorporeal life support) OR (secondary)), to retrieve original articles assessing different diagnostic criteria, definitions, and treatment of ECMO-CSI. Two authors (P.M. and C-E.L.) independently screened titles and abstracts to obtain relevant articles for full text review. We obtained the full text of all potentially relevant studies, and the scientific committee independently decided on final inclusion in the review. To ensure no relevant studies were missed, we also reviewed the references of relevant articles and

conducted a direct search in PubMed without using MeSH terms. Following this search, two reviewers (P.M. and C-E.L.) identified cohorts using different definitions of ECMO-CSI. We chose to exclude studies about ECMO BSI, leaving a total of 19 studies (see Table 1). To avoid influencing the experts’ answers, they were not shared with them. A flowchart is added in Supplemental Fig. S3. First, the review revealed significant heterogeneity in the definition of ECMO-CSI. In addition, only one study defined criteria for suspected ECMO-CSI, and the methodology for sampling was not defined in all studies. Furthermore, sampling was conducted using various methods, such as subcutaneous fine-needle aspiration or swab techniques. Lastly, the modalities of treatment (number of antimicrobials and duration of treatment, definition of treatment failure, need for cannula-site change, etc.) were reported in only one of the studies. This literature review identified six interrelated research areas, which were addressed thematically yet synchronously during the Delphi process: (i) clinical situations for possible ECMO-CSI, (ii) methodology for ECMO-CSI diagnosis, (iii) clinical criteria for ECMO-CSI definition, (iv) bacteriological criteria for ECMO-CSI, (v) ECMO-CSI treatment, and (vi) ECMO-CSI prevention.

Results Experts’ characteristics and Delphi process Among the 39 experts, 35 (90%) had > 10 years of experience in treating ECMO patients, the remaining 4 had 5–10  years of experience. Most experts (n = 35, 90%) worked in high-volume ECMO centers (> 30 ECMO/ year), the remaining four worked in medium-volume centers (10–30 ECMO/year). Most were intensivists, but surgeons, pulmonologists, and infectious disease specialists were also represented (Supplemental Table  S1). All experts participated in the first 2 rounds, and 38 participated in the last 2 rounds from October 2024 to June 2025 (Supplemental Fig.  S2). A summary of the iterative process followed to achieve consensus definitions of distinct parts of ECMO-CSI is shown in Supplemental Fig. S4. Full details of the four rounds of question are provided in the Electronic Supplementary Material (pages 13 to 128).

Definition of ECMO‑CSI Experts agreed on several situations defining ECMO- CSI (Fig. 1 and Supplemental Table S2). First, a pathogen must be systematically isolated through local microbiological sampling to define ECMO-CSI. Once a pathogen is isolated, the following situations were defined as ECMO-CSI: presence of a purulent discharge and/or inflammatory signs, regardless of any associated general or biological signs (except for immunosuppressed

Conversely, the experts agreed that hemodynamic instability or general and biological signs suggestive of infection, in the absence of local inflammatory signs or purulent discharge, should not be considered sufficient to define an ECMO-CSI, even in the presence of positive local cultures. Lastly, there was no consensus on defining a purulent discharge with a negative local microbiological sampling as an ECMO-CSI (50% of experts considered this as an ECMO-CSI).

Suspicion of ECMO‑CSI We obtained consensus on several clinical situations in which ECMO-CSI is suspected (Fig. 2 and Supplemental Table S3). The presence of purulent discharge alone, irrespective of local inflammatory signs or clinical and biological findings, was deemed sufficient by the experts to suspect an ECMO-CSI. Furthermore, local inflammatory signs associated with either general or biological signs of infection, hemodynamic instability, positive blood culture for a non-contaminant pathogen, or when the size of erythema at cannula insertion site is > 0.5 cm should raise suspicion for ECMO-CSI. In contrast, no consensus was reached in cases of local inflammatory signs without purulent discharge and without clinical or biological evidence of infection, as only 59% of experts would have suspected an ECMO-CSI in this context. Similarly, no consensus was reached in case of inflammatory signs without purulent discharge in immunosuppressed patient, as only 38% of experts would have suspected an ECMO-CSI in this context. Experts agreed that if there are no inflammatory signs at the ECMO insertion site, regardless of other clinical or biological signs, even if bacteremia is present, ECMO-CSI should not be suspected (76% agreement).

Methodology for ECMO‑CSI diagnosis Consensus was obtained on several points (Fig.  3 and Supplemental Table S4). First, when ECMO-CSI is suspected, a sample should be obtained from cannula site, whereas in the absence of suspected ECMO-CSI, neither systematic sampling of cannula sites nor systematic blood cultures should be performed. Second, experts agreed that a peripheral blood culture should be performed systematically in addition to local sampling when ECMO- CSI is suspected. However, experts agreed that blood

cultures alone (peripheral or from arterial/central lines) are not sufficient to diagnose ECMO-CSI (85% and 95%, respectively). There was no consensus whether blood cultures should be performed on the membrane lung to diagnose ECMO-CSI. In cases of purulent discharge, sampling can be performed using a sterile swab (77% agreement) or using a sterile plastic hub from an intravenous catheter mounted on a sterile syringe, inserted between the ECMO cannula and the subcutaneous space, followed by suctioning of purulent discharge (76% agreement) (see Supplemental Video S1). However, there was no consensus whether or not the cannula insertion site should be cleaned with antiseptic before sampling (68% of experts agreed on site disinfection before sampling). In the absence of purulent discharge (i.e., no discharge or non-purulent discharge), no consensus was achieved on the sampling methodology to be performed for diagnosing ECMO-CSI. Consensus was almost achieved regarding the use of sterile swab sampling in this situation (68% of agreement). In addition, 60% of experts agreed on the following procedure: insertion of the plastic hub of an intravenous catheter, mounted on a sterile syringe, through the entry port of the ECMO cannula into the subcutaneous space, followed by the injection of 1  mL of sterile saline and immediate aspiration (see Supplemental Video S2). However, puncture of the skin around the ECMO cannula was not recommended, regardless of the clinical presentation (79% against). Consensus was reached on the usefulness of sending the cannula tip for culture following ECMO removal in cases of ongoing ECMO-CSI, presence of purulent discharge at the time of decannulation, or cannula change due to suspected ECMO-CSI. No consensus was reached regarding the usefulness of sending the cannula tip for culture for other scenarios.

Bacteriology Consensus was reached to consider Enterococcus spp. and anaerobes as pathogens responsible for ECMO-CSI, alongside organisms not typically regarded as contaminants, such as Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Enterobacterales. Moreover, consensus was reached to consider coagulase-negative Staphylococcus as a pathogen responsible for ECMO-CSI in the following specific situations: when there were signs of inflammation and purulent discharge at the ECMO cannula site (i) associated with shock; or (ii) when a blood culture grew the same Staphylococcus strain (defined by an identical resistance profile) as the one found in a local sample. No consensus was reached to consider this pathogen as responsible for ECMO-CSI outside these two scenarios. Lastly, if a local sample yielded two or more pathogenic

Treatment of ECMO‑CSI Experts recommended an empirical treatment targeting both Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogens. Although no consensus was reached on whether Candida spp. should be considered a contaminant or a true pathogen, empiric antifungal therapy may be warranted in specific clinical situations (Supplemental Fig. S5). For definitive treatment, experts agreed that most pathogens can be managed with a single antimicrobial agent, except difficult-to-treat Pseudomonas and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales in immunosuppressed patients, for which no consensus was reached regarding the number of antimicrobials to use (Supplemental Fig. S6). The duration of definitive treatment was not consensual among experts except for some pathogens (Supplemental Fig. S6), but a consensus was reached regarding the need for an infectious disease specialist advice to tailor the duration and choice of antimicrobials.

ECMO‑CSI treatment failure Experts reached a consensus on defining ECMO-CSI treatment failure (Supplemental Figs. S7 and S8), which included new or persistent purulent discharge from the cannula insertion site, lack of improvement or progression of inflammatory signs, lack of improvement in hemodynamic status, or persistent positive blood cultures. However, no consensus was reached regarding the timeframe for defining treatment failure. Similarly, there was no consensus on whether a lack of improvement in general clinical or biological parameters should be considered indicative of treatment failure. To confirm treatment failure, experts agreed that a new local sample should be taken for microbiological documentation (71% agreement). In cases where microbiological results were negative, there was consensus against changing the cannula site. However, no consensus was reached on changing the cannula site in case of a positive new sample, whatever the clinical situation. Experts only recommended changing the ECMO cannula site in cases of persistent bloodstream infection with the same pathogen identified at the cannula site.

Prevention of ECMO‑CSI We reached consensus against the use of antimicrobial prophylaxis for percutaneous ECMO cannulation, and when ECMO is implanted surgically in the operating room, in the cardiac catheterization laboratory or in the ICU (Fig. 4 and Supplemental Table S5). There was a consensus in favor of antibiotic prophylaxis when ECMO is implanted surgically under extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation ECPR or in conditions other than the settings cited before. Experts also recommended antibiotic prophylaxis when an ECMO cannula—where the insertion site shows signs of inflammation—is advanced into the patient (74% of agreement), whereas there was consensus against the use of antimicrobial prophylaxis in other situations requiring cannula manipulation (pull back or advancement without local inflammatory signs). Consensus was reached to recommend the use of chlorhexidine-impregnated dressings on cannula insertion site (74% agreement) or transparent, sterile, semipermeable polyurethane dressings when the former was not available (90% agreement), which should remain unchanged (for both kinds of dressing) until day 7 unless soiled by blood, dirt, or moisture. Lastly, there was consensus against the systematic use of systemic digestive decontamination to prevent ICU-acquired bacteremia and ECMO-CSI (90% disagreement).

Discussion Using the Delphi method to elicit opinions from a panel of 39 international experts, we developed a consensus on the definitions, clinical criteria, and management strategies (including prevention) for ECMO-CSI. Despite its frequency, the diagnosis and management of ECMO-CSI remain poorly standardized in the literature, with heterogeneity in definitions and therapeutic approaches among studies. Our study provides a foundational framework that could standardize future research and clinical practice in this area. The main finding of this study is the consensus regarding definition of ECMO-CSI. There was agreement that it should be limited to patients presenting both a positive culture of local sample and local signs of inflammation, with or without purulent discharge. Conversely, patients with positive local microbiological cultures but without inflammatory signs should be classified as colonized rather than infected. Similarly, patients with local inflammatory signs but negative microbiological cultures should not be considered infected. This distinction between infection and colonization is crucial from an antimicrobial stewardship perspective, because it may help prevent unnecessary antibiotic use [28]. The present definition of ECMO-CSI was close to that of Aslam et al. for their definition of vascular-site infection [29], except

that they split it into uncomplicated and complicated, according to the presence or not of systemic signs of infection, positive blood cultures, or multidrug-resistant pathogen; and to the definition of peripheral ECMO-site infection in children proposed by Alexander et al., which was defined as a positive culture from the skin surrounding the ECMO cannula when there is clinical evidence of infection such as pain, drainage, erythema, or leukocytosis [30]. Another important finding is related to ECMO-CSI suspicion: irrespective of other clinical signs, purulent discharge and local inflammatory signs are the main criteria to suspect ECMO-CSI. Moreover, ECMO-CSI should not be suspected in the absence of local inflammatory signs and/or purulent discharge, regardless of other clinical or biological signs. We provide clear guidance for clinicians, which may be crucial for timely and accurate diagnosis, and to avoid inaccurate sampling, which may lead to over-treatment of colonized patients. Although experts recommend local sampling in cases of purulent discharge—using one of two preferred methods, either swabbing or aspiration with a plastic hub along the cannula—they advise against systematic sampling of the cannula insertion site, even in the presence of bacteremia, as well as against certain sampling techniques, such as percutaneous skin puncture around the cannula. However, no consensus could be reached regarding sampling strategies in the absence of purulent discharge. It was challenging to unequivocally define the bacteriological aspects of ECMO-CSI unequivocally. The experts agreed on considering common ICU pathogens but also highlighted specific situations where coagulase-negative Staphylococcus should be considered pathogenic. This nuanced approach reflects the complexity of managing infections in critically ill patients and the need for individualized assessment. In terms of ECMO-CSI treatment, empiric treatment targeting both Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogens, and empiric antifungals in specific situations is recommended. Whereas experts agreed on the use of single agent in most cases, no consensus was found on the duration of antimicrobial treatment, highlighting the need for further research and individualized patient care. The prevention of ECMO-CSI was in line with central line infection guidelines: chlorhexidine-impregnated or semipermeable polyurethane dressings, unchanged for 7  days unless soiled or bleeding. While up to 40% of patients receive prophylactic antimicrobials during cannulation [31], and some recommend it for surgical ECMO (i.e., open cannulations) [32], our expert panel advise against routine antimicrobial prophylaxis during ECMO insertion, except for open cannulation in specific

situations: during ECPR, or when ECMO is implanted outside operating room, cardiac catheterization laboratory or ICU. This study has several limitations. First, the subjectivity inherent in the Delphi method is a primary concern. However, we provided several guarantees of objectivity, including transparency in the Delphi process, optimization of open-ended questions, and the possibility of free comments. Our expert panel included ICU physicians with extensive ECMO experience from geographically diverse backgrounds, including both high- and middle-income countries. While representation from low-income settings was limited, the panel’s composition still reflects a broad range of expertise and clinical contexts. Second, some clinical situations were not consensual. As an example, in the absence of purulent discharge (no discharge, non-purulent discharge) but with local inflammatory signs, no consensus was found on the sampling methodology to be performed for diagnosing ECMO-CSI. We were also not able to find consensus on the duration of antimicrobial treatment for ECMO-CSI. We, therefore, cannot give recommendations to clinicians regarding these specific situations. This lack of consensus highlights a critical gap between clinical signs and microbiological confirmation. Similarly,

cases with inflammatory signs but negative cultures also remain diagnostically unclear. These scenarios reflect real-world dilemmas and underscore the need for further prospective studies to refine and validate the diagnostic criteria established in this consensus. Third, because the literature on ECMO-CSI is limited, our recommendations are mostly based on clinical experience. Unlike previous studies on broader adverse events or devices like ventricular assist devices [29, 30], we also focus on the suspicion, prevention, and treatment of peripheral ECMO-CSI. Therefore, the opinion of experts may be affected by differences in other aspects of care relevant to their healthcare setting. As an example, the results of a recently finished but not yet published trial evaluating chlorhexidine-impregnated dressing to prevent ECMO- CSI (NCT05750576) may or may not be consistent with our recommendations. Another limitation concerns the uncertainty surrounding sampling methodologies, especially in cases without purulent discharge. Although consensus was achieved regarding the collection of purulent material—whether by swabbing or plastic hub aspiration—the optimal strategy in the absence of discharge remains undefined. Furthermore, no agreement was reached on whether the sampling site should be disinfected prior to collection, even when discharge is present.

These gaps underscore the lack of standardized operating procedures, which may contribute to variability in clinical practice. Addressing these unresolved issues will require both harmonization of sampling protocols and prospective studies to assess the diagnostic yield and clinical impact of the different techniques. This Delphi study also has several strengths. It represents a significant step towards standardizing the definitions and diagnostic criteria for peripheral ECMO-CSI, which could enhance intra- and interdepartmental communication and support both patient management and research in this area. The international composition of the expert panel and the representation of all world regions strengthens the credibility of this consensus, providing a robust foundation for future guidelines and clinical practice.

Conclusion This Delphi study enabled us to reach an expert consensus on the definition, diagnostic criteria, and management strategies for peripheral ECMO-CSI. This consensus is a crucial step towards standardizing judgment criteria for future research and clinical trials, ultimately improving patient outcomes in this complex and challenging field.
